newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian pharmacists up in arms over budget. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Italian pharmacists up in arms over budget. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: Private Italian pharmacists, accusing the government of seeking to slash their profit margins, have said they will no longer help local health authorities regulate subsidies on medicine costs.

At present, chemists charge Italians lower-than-cost prices for a range of state-approved pharmaceutical products. The chemists then obtain reimbursements from the state health service, but do not receive full payment for the drugs.

The health service currently enjoys a three percent discount on the retail value of the drugs, but in its 1997 budget, the government announced it was introducing five new discount bands ranging from 2.5 percent to 10.5 percent.
Thus, if a medicine officially costs 100,000 lire ($65.69), from next year the government will pay only 89,500 lire (Corrects from 895,000 lire) for the drug.

The federation of private chemists predicts that the new regime will cost its members some 160 billion lire a year and decided at a meeting on Sunday to charge customers the full cost for all their medicines from October 28.
This means that people will have to go themselves to the local authorities to get reimbursements on prescription costs.
The decision could bring chaos to the health service and the government accused the chemists' federation, which represents some 16,000 pharmacists, of acting irresponsibly.
"Chemists' earnings have risen by around 600 billion lire this year...and we are now asking them for a little contribution," Health Minister Rosi Bindi told reporters.

She added that chemists currently enjoyed a 26 percent mark-up on medicine prices and said that the government was letting private pharmacists sell expensive, potentially lucrative drugs next year, such as new treatment for Aids.
Italy's 2,000 municipal chemists will not take part in the protest.
The 1997 budget is currently being examined at commission stage in the lower house of parliament and has to be ratified by both houses of parliament by the end of the year.
